As someone who worked for Samsung inside Costco's to sell TVs... OLED from Samsung (QD-OLED) is the winning choice. For a TV. For a monitor? IPS/mini LED is still the way to go. There are people who have done tests on OLED and tried to recommend best practices, ect... but real world does not stop in the middle of a game stream so you can pixel shift your display to 'condition it.' '

Woled is the worst kind of OLED, because it uses a white light to produce the image (a 4th white pixel exists). QD OLED is RGB pixels only. Even on the best of LG displays, the blacks get crushed hard by the panel, while the highlights tend to over bloom and color band. While Tandem OLED is supposed to solve burn-in problems, it's done by stacking panels on top of each other, using additional layers. 

I recently upgraded to mini led IPS display as my main monitor, and it's much much better than OLED... I have OLED on my phone display... it's not impressive.

comments.text:
​ @VividlyHeejin kind of a misunderstanding of the tech. QD oled is simply Samsungs Quantum Dot Oled. WOLED is simply LGs version of Oled. Both companies sell their panels to other companies to make monitors and TVs.

QD uses a sub pixel arrangement of red, blue, green. There is no black pixel or black filter applied. What you are seeing is the natural black level of... Oled. The reason you don't see that on WOLED is because WOLED used RGB sub pixels with a 4th white pixel added. 

QD oled is blue filtered, WOLED is yellow filtered. Meaning any QD oled panel is going to be using a blue light filter with red and green sub pixels resulting in a true color image... where oled/tandem oled are going to be using a yellow filter to add brightness with a white sub pixel in addition to RGB. 

Side by side under a microscope, the pixel arrangement of QD oled looks color accurate to RGB. The WOLED looks very washed out and RGB looks more like 'red green brown' with a white pixel in there. 

If you prefer a brighter overall image, that's cool. WOLED all day i guess. If you prefer something more color accurate, QD oled. If you want to see QD oled with an additional filter applied, go look at a Sony bravia Oled. Literally added a filter for image darkening and it shows. 

Right now HDR sucks. It's just not a good tech. SDR on a mini led with local dimming enabled is a much better experience depending on the game. 

I play SDR on an IPS without local dimming for some games. Other games, where the lighting and realism are important... SDR with local dimming.

comments.text:
@VividlyHeejin  Says I'm using 'outdated information' but then calls mini led 'VA.' I have an IPS mini LED. IPS is not VA. Mini LED means it has local dimming zones and can effectively control the lighting for dynamic scenes, much like an OLED can. Add to that the great overall picture quality and contrast of a fast IPS, it becomes difficult to justify an OLED. 

No amount of updated features are going to change the nature of OLED... it's organic light emitting diode. Meaning it has a limited life span no matter how much time you spend trying to refresh pixels or shift constant ui elements... blue pixels have the shortest lifespan, once they lose their ability to react to voltage... then they don't look so good. 

Where if I just find a quality IPS panel to use... not organic, can last upward of 10-20 years without losing pixel clarity, color, or brightness. 

The Mini LED I just bought replaced a monitor with 20k on use hours.... that still looks brand new. I don't think any OLED will ever last that long.

comments.text: RGB stripe also significantly improves the banding issues on W-OLED. Typical W-OLED displays have an RGWB stripe subpixel layout, where there's a dedicated white subpixel. Similar to how the triangular subpixel layout screws with the way computers expect text to be rendered, having that extra white subpixel screws with how large fields of solid color are rendered, and banding is a common side effect. W-OLED panels with just RGB stripe and no extra white subpixel are starting to come out (the new AW3926QW is one of the first ones, and initial reviews have shown it to be much improved in this respect).

comments.text:
@VividlyHeejin  Um. HDR in windows is awful. You  ever tried using it? SDR with local dimming tends to look better (visually) than with HDR enabled. Also: I run in 10 bit color mode at slightly lower FPS cap with display port 1.4. 

I didn't need chat GPT to respond to randoms on this subject... SDR just means 'standard dynamic range' content... which is just normal stuff. 

Local dimming is controlled by the monitor itself (simply turn it on/off, depending on the quality of your monitor I guess) and it definitely makes a difference even without HDR enabled in windows. 

A game like GTA 5 is a perfect example. Playing on Enhanced with RTX enabled, local dimming disabled, SDR: Game looks slightly better than with RTX off, but still looks like a 'video game' with the lighting (not very dynamic). But with Local Dimming set to Medium-smooth, the panel adjusts lighting... locally xD. 

The result is a much more realistic image with dynamic lighting and near OLED level blacks. The only thing that still isn't quite as good as OLED is the pixel response time. Sub 1ms is good, but still slower than OLED (because pixels still shift between colors and gradients, while OLED is controlling those factors by each pixel). It's probably not possible for IPS to reach the level of pixel refresh of OLED, but does have the advantages of not being limited lifespan Organic, like OLED.

This generation of kids really needs just stfu and push buttons on things to learn something. If you think I used Chat GPT here... I say your understanding of OLED came from a youtube short generated by AI. 

I wouldn't personally buy an OLED monitor for daily use, but other people have. I am not saying they shouldn't, I'm saying there are trade-offs and nothing about the tech has solved the burn in problem without significant upkeep, even if it's mostly automated and conventient now. 

The pixels still burn in, grayscales still look kinda awful (I thought my 24GN650-b looked bad in grayscale, OLED somehow looks worse) and my 25m2s has slight blooming on a completely black screen in a couple spots (with local dimming off) but when I turn on that local dimming... it's almost magic. 

Unexpectedly. It's also a 24.5 inch 1440p resolution. That combination... is simply unavailable in OLED. I sit too close to my monitors for something bigger (used to have 2x 27 inch, had a 32 inch, they were too big). 2x 24 inch is perfect for my usage case.

This video is extremely misinformed in regards to Banding, Vertical Banding may disappear almost entirely over time, the biggest issue with it was the early 6 months of batches, theyve since refineda nd improved it massively, its ofcourse no guarantee you'll get a flawless panel, hardly anyone ever will, but once you recieve your unit you are asked by Asus/Gigabyte whatever to run a pixel clean, once before actual use, if you dont you'll notice very obvious vertical bands against a very specific few shades of darkest grays (aswell as pixel width thin lines that go alongside these bars) after teh clean, on my unit, all bands vanished (XG27AQWMG) and the monitor looked almost identical to my PG279Q IPS in regards to gray uniformity. Keep in mind even if it doesnt all vanish on the first one, it may do so within the first 100 hours of use (thats like 10 days for work from home/gamers) or 2-3 weeks for a "4 h a day" user. And in most first world countries we have good return policies, not happy? Return within 30 days, 60 days, 90 days (Sweden) open box. So its not like a money thrown into fire situation. If it doesnt improve at all (i.e. to the point of being usable in all scenarios) then you just return it, you either try a new model or ask for your money back, no fuss here atleast. 

Getting upset that discord doesnt look completely uniform is funny though. Who runs discord in fullscreen theres so much meaningless dead space. Discord does not need to be wider than the Grid of embedded images for text messages and you certainly dont need to keep the members tab open ever. Regardless, dont buy anything except CRT if youre bothered by various issues: Banding, Clouding, DSE, Grid, Dithering, VRR Flickering. All of which may appear on: TN, IPS, VA, MINILED (IPS/VA), OLED and QDOLED monitors.

Also, what these videos NEVER tell you is that they OVER EXPOSE the photos (either unknowingly or knowingly to exaggerate the problem massively, and viewers, dont figure this out on their own, even when they can see the overexposure clear as day, the text literally glowing should be a hint) and the guy doesnt even tell us whether he ran the first initial pixel clean or not. We also dont know how old his monitor is and when he bought it (such as the batch) this video lacks so much information and just seem sensationalist, like hes trying to hit the algorithm.
QDOLED monitors also have a form of this except its a GRID that goes horizontal and vertical, these bands are much smaller, usually around 3-10 pixels in height/width and are completely random, and may shift around depending on the pixelclean (that you do atleast once per day, either manually or in standby/off). QDOLED monitors also come with VERTICAL DITHERING lines (its very LOCALIZED) and occurs in dark parts of an image, in particular when brightness is below 100% (but also happens in HDR) in again dark parts of a scene. Was very noticable in Cyberpunk at night against dark reds, magentas etc, aswell as Dead Island 2, this was on 4 separate QDOLED Monitor MODELS btw. Its never been improved since its an issue inherent to the panels. The Vertical lines are effectively the same as the DIAGONAL lines you can find on LG B/C/G series from the B3 and onwards. Though TV owners usually dont notice it as much since they sit over in africa to view their displays. Both technologies (WOLED and QDOLED) come with VRR Flicker. WOLEDs usually tend to have slightly less and the TVs have the least amount of VRR flicker, C5 42 had none when I used it paired with Gsync in the 144hz mode.

Also why is this guy using an OLED to browse discord?  
You buy OLED displays to use it as a MEDIA display primarily (games movies youtube twitch, light cad/productivity work). You place it in your center of the desk. You then use any other monitor, you know, 99% of us come from a PREVIOUS monitor or sets of monitors, that we then use as SECONDARY monitors, where you know, we have discord on and browsers and spotify and what not without any risk of burn in. "bbut my ddesk can only ffit one mmonitor.." almost like arms were never invented or something.

I also love the Miniled marketers in the comments spewing as if Miniled is somehow free from issues, and its obvious theyre really poor. Because you know OLEDs come with 3+ year burn in warranties meaning if your monitor were to somehow get burn in in 3 years (unlikely) you'll just get a new one in 3 years and that will last you another 3 years meaning 6+ years of use, for $500 (XG27AQWMG is really cheap btw) with no downsides really besides muh 1000ni t fullscreen that only minileds can achieve. That no one ever needed and no content actually makes use of. 99% of hdr movies and series are mastered for around 100-400 nits average brightness in a scene with only specific highlights going beyond that. (mad max fury road reserves most of these bright highlights for the lightning in the sandstorm for example)

Minileds out of the box: DSE, Clouding, VRR Flicker just like OLED, Grainy coatings because theyre always Matte making bright colors appear grainy or hazy. Local Dimming ZONE Flickering. Local Dimming ALGORITHM tuned only for when the display gets an HDR signal. in SDR content it doesnt work anywhere near as good as it does in HDR. So in order to use local dimming for desktop and sdr content you need to enable HDR and you need to go to git gud hub to fix the gamma issues. Youre still going to get Bloom and Inverse Blooming in desktop use. Not to mention most miniled IPS panels are slower than normal IPS equivalents without miniled backlight and sometimes as bad as VA panels when it comes to pixel response. Minileds with VA panels have pixelnoise in motion and black smear (theyve yet to eliminate this fully). Not to mention all VA monitors have bad viewing angles even when sat head on, you get a cone view of proper correct gamma in the center and then in a cone outside of this center you get a wash out that gets worse the closer to the edge youre looking (your head remains static in position, otherwise this will all shift) If you lean back in your chair watching a dark or dim movie/game the experience will shift overall because VAs dont allow you to move around without shifting gamma. IPS monitors have IPS Glow still as miniled monitors, its massively reduced when you have the local dimming enabled, but when you turn it off, its a normal IPS; typically with more bleeding and glow than a normal IPS.

If youre stingy and paranoid just stick with a regular fast ips.

If your desk somehow cant fit two or three displays, dont bother with anything past a regular fast ips or an ultrawide ips.

comments.text: Sorry you had such bad luck. I just bought the MSI MAG 341CQP QD-OLED X28 34” in an early black friday deal (£550 all in) and it's been great so far. The only issues are that if a game (like wow, which is cpu bottlenecked) is running below the VRR threshold, you get flickering, but lowering the refresh to 120Hz sorted that out. The other issue is you do need to look after the screen to avoid burn in, but most of that is handled by it's built in software. I just use the colour cycling option every four hours (it only takes 5 mins) to make sure and set my screen to turn off after 5 mins on no use. But all of the other issues are more or less fixed tbh, the text is perfect on it for example, no fringing anymore. The ultra wide screen is used a lot in wow as the HDR which looks great and in youtube videos that don't use up all of the screen, the sides just turn off and are fully black, no biggie at all. Excellent purchase so far, I waited like you for years before finding a screen that ticked most of the boxes and it was worth the wait.

comments.text:
I also did a lot of research before buying an OLED and had many of the same concerns as you did. I think it's the true the tech is not fully mature yet and they need to work out the issues, but my perspective after trying a 280hz tandem OLED is that at least for me, the benefits from OLED are so good that I can live with the issues. Picture quality, contrast ratio, and motion clarity is just so much better than any IPS I've tried. I was also eyeing mini-LEDs but quite frankly I was not that impressed by the one I tried, it only felt like a modest improvement over traditional LCDs whereas OLED actually feels like a true upgrade.

I also think I got somewhat lucky with my unit, as the grey banding is not noticeable except at pretty low greyscales so it's almost impossible for me to notice it during day to day use. The dirty screen effect is definitely there but given I used it mostly for games/videos and rarely for non-black static backgrounds it doesn't really bother me. If I got a bad unit I might be saying something totally different, though this is also why I made sure to purchase my monitor through a retailer that allows free 30-day returns.

Also glad you covered the text fringing issue because it's super true that there's really no good solution on windows. Even though tandem woled is better than qd-oled, there's still very visible text fringing issues on it. I spent quite some time wrangling with mactype tuner and better cleartype tuner and found that while mactype can fix the text rendering in certain apps, fixing it in some apps will also completely break text rendering in other apps so it's really not a viable solution. The tuning you can get from better cleartype tuner is too limited to truly fix the text rendering. Personally, I ended up just using greyscale rendering and living with the somewhat blocky text in some places because at least it gets rid of all the fringing everywhere and doesn't break text anywhere. I think this is all really a windows issue since windows text rendering is heavily optimized for RGB sub-pixels, but unfortunately if they never add support for other sub-pixel layouts this will remain an issue.

comments.text:
Maybe think with your brain and not your wallet next time?...
I went from a 24 inch 1080p IPS to a 27 inch 1440p 3rd gen QD-OLED and I did notice a slight increase in image clarity
In the first few days I used it, the text color fringing was noticeable, now I got used to it and it's a non-issue
Jokes on you, I used it on light mode for the first 2 months, after doing a power consumption test while displaying various shades of gray and different images, I realized I can halve the draw (and relax my eyes) by using dark colors, the color fringing doesn't bother me at all, and I code
Expecting a weirdly shaped subpixel layout on the OLED to perform like the RGB stripe one on the LCD is nuts
The only way to attack this problem is increasing PPI massively (either by shrinking the diagonal at the same resolution or by increasing the resolution above 4K at the same diagonal)
Also, do your research properly, on your own, about the tech, tech reviewers are salesmen with extra steps, WOLED has the issues it's plagued with due to the white subpixel and how it's powered relative to its siblings from other pixel column groups
Gray is a very difficult color to reproduce by any OLED due to how fine grained the pixel current control has to be for each subpixel
If you get a QD-OLED, you have to learn to accept purple-ish blacks in the day and minimize room brightness in the evening to truly enjoy the infinite contrast
With the currently available tech, QD-OLEDs can't get bright enough to overpower a polarizer layer and WOLED introduce such a big issue (banding, amongst others) to solve it
Maybe experiencing a 27 inch 1440p or 4K IPS would've changed my opinion on clarity, but the other issues an LCD has (uneven brightness (which leads to uneven colors), vignette effect, ghosting (which can be solved with BFI most manufacturers implement), gray blacks) are by far worse than the OLED downsides (of current gen panels, early adopters are scammed beta testers, it's the same for every new technology these days)

comments.text: Mactype doesn't just allow greyscale font smoothing, it more importantly also allows you to define your own subpixel layout (essentially any subpixel layout, see Freetype 2 documentation), at least in recent versions. The problem with Mactype however is that it's best at hooking into the old GDI font rendering and struggles (not for any fault of its own, it's just much harder or almost impossible to do) with the newer DirectWrite rendering that is used more and more in Windows, most notably in browsers. So its usability is limited.

comments.text:
Hi, I’d like to share my own experience. My first OLED monitor was the ASUS PG27CDM, and just like you mentioned, there was noticeable fringing around text. However, the biggest issue for me was how incredibly sensitive glossy screens are to scratches, fingerprints, and dirt.

After doing a few hours of research, I found that Samsung was basically the only manufacturer using a matte coating on these panels, so I went ahead and bought one. I can comfortably say that text looks noticeably cleaner and sharper compared to glossy OLEDs. Of course, you can still see some green and pink fringing around text, but compared to glossy panels, I find it much more satisfying and most of the time I don’t even notice it.

The main downside of the matte coating is that it doesn’t look quite as visually impressive as glossy, and when looking at a completely white page, you can notice a slightly grainy texture from the coating.

I’m currently using the 27-inch Samsung G81SF, but if you want a QD-OLED with a less aggressive matte coating, you could also take a look at the Samsung G80SD, which uses a 3rd-gen QD-OLED panel.

comments.text:
VRR flicker is my biggest gripe with OLED panels, and is ultimately the entire reason I'm still on a regular IPS monitor and haven't upgraded to OLED. It's infuriating to see so many people online brush it off by saying that they only notice it in menus, or they just turn off VRR completely because the flicker is horrible. Turning VRR off is not a solution. Then you'll see other people say, "just cap your frames lol". That is also NOT a solution. Capping your fps will do nothing to fix VRR flicker if the game your playing has an unstable frametime even if the frames are capped. And then you'll see people go into this whole monologue about all the software they use to stabilize frametimes and eliminate flicker, and it just sounds exhausting. You shouldn't have to do all that for every game you play. And what's even worse is popular reviewers recommending these panels despite having horrible VRR flicker. 

I fell into that trap once with the AOC Q27G3XMN, a VA Mini-LED monitor. RTINGS gave it a great review despite it having the worst VRR flicker of ANY panel they had EVER tested. I bought one, thinking maybe it wouldn't bother me that much, but I was wrong lol. I don't think I'll ever be purchasing an OLED until there's some sort of tech that eliminates VRR flicker without introducing another equally annoying drawback.

i had a similar journey starting in, i think late march. i bought the asus 27in 1440p 280hz tandem. out of the box it had horrendous gray banding, but thats kinda normal. after just one pixel refresh, about 80% of it was gone. over time it became less and less. but dse seemed to become worse and worse. i only learned about the batches later on so i dont know if i got the good or bad batch. id assume it was the bad batch. i think i had it for little over 2 weeks and returned it. oh yeah and the neo prox sensor was crap. didnt work properly. it would shut off no matter what distance i set it to. would happen to me mid match/game so i just turned it off. but aside from that, the deep blacks and the trueblack glossy clarity was amazing.

next i tried qd oled it was the msi MAG 272QP QD-OLED X50. also 27in 1440p, but with 500hz. checked uniformity, it was pretty much perfect. maybe u could say u could see a super tiny bit of dse if u used a specific grayscale and put ur eyeballs on the monitor, but it was realistically perfect. the text fringing was noticeable tho and felt like it was fucking with my eyes. i forgot how i came across it, but i found posts and discussions on reddit about eye strain from qd oled. doesnt seem to affect everyone, but some stated much higher eye strain from qd oled. saying things like it would feel like it was searing their eyes, red eyes, headaches, and poor sleep. i actually did notice i was experiencing all of the above aside from the sleep prob since im always sleep deprived anyway. many of those ppl reported the issues going away when switching over to woled. but as for visuals, it was nice and vibrant with the colors. the raised black levels was definitely an issue for me tho. i have lamp behind me, which isnt super bright, but i also have white walls that would bounce some sunlight, and also i use a monitor light bar. i noticed the warmer the lighting, the more purple the blacks would become. my light bar has a slider for warmer or colder light. also i felt that the bfi was unusable because of the lack of brightness, but it was smooth. compared to the tandem which in order to use bfi, u would have to half the framerate unfortunately. 

i started deciding if maybe i should just go 3rd gen woled. then decided that i really liked tandem oled as the brightness really hit for when i was viewing hdr oled videos plus the trueblack glossy coating. the better lifespan was an added bonus. so i just went for trying the lottery again. this time i went for the gigabyte model since idgaf about the neo prox sensor and the gigabyte model was a bit cheaper. again out of the box there was banding, but very little dse. good start as dse is more what i was worried about. pixel refresh pretty much gets rid of the banding. dse is still there ofc, but is quite minimal. overall it was good enough so i decided to keep it after continuing to trial it. im 734hrs and 114 pixel cleans in now. dse and banding is pretty much a non issue. i can see it very slightly occasionally, but its almost never noticeable in any actual content. only thing is that i think part of  the cost difference from the asus is the display bandwith. the asus can do the full 280hz without dsc, but the gigabyte only does 200hz without dsc.not a huge deal, but i do notice that it has significantly longer wake times than anything ive ever used. even with dsc off. but ive largely just been dealing with it. its not the end of the world. just a few more seconds. overall pretty happy with it tho. the new hypernits feature is pretty nice too. just wish that the state of hdr in games wasnt so shit.

comments.text:
I can only say that OLED is quite disappointing to me, as someone that tried a bunch of them in the past two years and always returned them. (inkl. the 2:03 1440p ROG Strix Tandem)
Apart from texts looking ass and grey-banding (what was never that big an issue to me), my main issue were color-shifts and the fact that in real everyday situations it simply never looked that much better than my <$150 IPS screen.
Especially the color shifts were irritating. Wood and darker skincolors became literally chocolate, a lot of things that are meant to be blue would turn teal/turquoise colored and some colors were just aggresively so more saturated than others. Its like you are getting a monitor out of the box with a "showroom calibration". And unless ones brain connect "a lot of strong colors = better", all of them just looked like trash out of the box. Non-Tandem WOLEDs were honestly the least bad, simply because they had less strong colors, due to the screen-tech.
What i loved were the blacks in the few situations, where one would actually see 0% dark blacks or high contrast content and the clear image. But none of it in comparison with the issues all of them have would be worth $300-$500 to me. And looking at how many of the shops (Germany) have boatloads of returner-devices severely discounted, the disappointement seems to be quite widespread.
My next attempt will be an RGB-stripe OLED, when they come down in price. Everything else, i wouldnt even consider, until they drop below 200-250 bucks.

I don't use OLED because the organic LED layer means quick degradation and after the experience with burn-in on my Motorola AMOLED phone just no...
MicroLED fixes that flaw but it's unobtanium and there are other problems. Instead my secondary monitor is a FHD IPS LCD and my primary one is a mid high end 19inch Samsung Syncmaster 955DF AN19J CRT  monitor from 2003. 

This Samsung CRT is a gem because it has a real dotpitch of 0.2309mm  around 127PPI and a max res of 1536p. 
I found it intact after almost 17 years without any usage, it's symmetrical round phosphor dot mask and the text clarity is just like QHD 27inch digital LCD, very impressive brightness for such an old CRT (hard to find CRTs in a mint condition without degradation of the anode/cathode with a brightness loss). 
I missed the perfect motion clarity, lack of input lag and the HDR-like look of CRT and no aliasing (analog). I don't care about HDR support (and the CRT because of being analog doesn't need it anyways), it's a dumpster fire.

Finally the hard truth: digital screens suck in gaming vs this 23 year old CRT monitor . I did tried gaming on a Samsung S90C QD OLED TV but the motion clarity is so much worse at 144Hz vs my CRT at 60 and banding on SDR is extremely noticiable, it does have a bigger dynamic range but overall i will never use an OLED with a PC.

I also have roughly the space for two 27" monitors on my desk. Around 4~5 years ago I decided to get a LG C1 48", the same horizontal space as two 24", as a monitor for mixed media and programming. This year I switched to a G6 55". (Banding is basically imperceptible on my unit unless I squint.) OLED monitors aside, I'd still vouch for the cult (?) of using a single OLED TV to replace a multi-display setup. Even if clarity is a concern, a 42" C6 still has higher PPI than a 2k 27" monitor, and it's awesome to have just the content in front of you without bezels in the center.

Here’s my experience with my first OLED, as I have not had these issues. I want to recommend my monitor and tell you my experience. 

Despite the recent controversy about the adware problem, I’ve been a happy LG user for years and have grown fond of the menu UI.

I recently went from an LG 165hz 27” IPS, to a 27” LG WOLED with a GLOSSY panel and 240hz (both were 1440p) 

I was looking up best settings and practices with my new monitor. I had clicked on a google ai response to one of my searches , it opened up the Google Ai site in dark mode. Vertical banding was extremely noticeable. I couldn’t believe it. I got really nervous and began to research it. 

Apparently this is common with these monitors when they are brand new , but I read it will goes away. So, I did pixel cleaning cycle, did some video editing in Davinci resolve for an hour, played a game for an hour, then BOOM. It disappeared completely, no vertical banding.

I did grey scale testing and have used the monitor a lot for a couple of weeks now. There is no vertical banding at all and hasn’t been since I spent a couple hours with it.

This monitor was on sale recently for $380 on Amazon. I think regular pricing is closer to $499? 

At 90% brightness and peak brightness set to medium even, the monitor is EXTREMELY bright. 

The color calibration is immaculate, and I see no difference in text.

I’ve played games, read articles, edited full videos, did Lightroom photo editing, and did a lot of music production work in ableton. All were fantastic experiences.

I hope this is helpful! The monitor model is 27GX704a-b … I also want to ask how long did you have the first monitor that had the banding issue?? Maybe I missed that detail, but I wonder if perhaps it had may have improved with usage as well

Hey man, I have an aw3225q; 3rd gen qd-oled. I am the kind of person who notices the smallest issues and hyperfixates. I use my monitor for productivity, gaming, and engineering, and I actually bought it used (technically... i think the seller got a new model from the dell warranty).

I was extremely proud of owning what I thought was an incredible, endgame monitor. And the colors were unlike anything on my budget VA. But I do remember that the moment I booted up windows on this new monitor, I was like... what am I looking at. For some reason, the text just looked so odd. I searched up the pixel density compared to my phone and laptop, and I just decided that that was the issue, and moved on.

Recently, with the huge price cuts in OLED monitors recently, I've realized I didn't get the very best monitor or deal. I considered selling my aw3225qf and then using that monitor to sponsor a better panel. 

But then, I took a second to relax, and compared my new and old monitor, and I realized that my 3rd gen QD-OLED panel was absolutely beautiful, despite not being the brightest or best hdr implementation. 

Even now, I learned for your video that the reason the text looks weird (mind you I use dark mode for everything) is because of the color fringing. I looked close at the text, and I saw exactly what you showed. But even now, I have gotten used to it after months of ownership, and it doesn't bother me compared to how gorgeous video games and movies look now. 

I don't think this video is ragebait, so I really wonder, how is this not enough for you? Yes, there's a chance your eyes are simply more sensitive to the color fringing than mine. You probably sit closer considering your monitor is smaller. But I feel like you have become noseblind to the benefits of improvement in your technology. I enjoyed your video nonetheless, but I really wish you'd put your 1440p and 4k panel side-by-side and tell me you can't be happy with the improvements in video, gaming, and certain productivity tasks. 

(I am not talking about Tandem OLEDs in this spiel. I think the panel lottery and the greyscale banding is a stupid thing for paying that much money, for what, a slightly brighter, more contrasting screen?)

comments.text:
I completely disagree with your take on the color fringing. Not only is it much less noticeable as resolutions rise (naturally, since subpixels are relatively smaller), it's also almost entirely a learned thing.  You'll get used to it.  Prior text-rendering tech had issues too; notably cleartype always introduces color fringing, by design, since that's clearer on a vertical stripe LCD display (and people complained about that, too!).  Prior to cleartype, fonts were often aliased, which is another flaw, and yet still readable. And that's the point of text - to be readable. On a QD-OLED with cleartype set to grayscale (i.e. no EXTRA color-fringing), text is clearly legible, although not as clear as on an LCD with cleartype.  But you've tried a 1.5x scale by the sounds of it - a 2160p display rather than a 1440p, and the res difference probably fully compensates.  You can definitely read such text clearly, and will get used to it.  If it bothers you as much as you're describing, it sounds to me likely you're triggered more by the change than in any reasonable way proportional to the problem.

Sure, it's a downside; but the description in the video and especially the unreasonable closeups just misrepresent how you'll use a display.  If you're staring at text so closely each subpixel is a very clearly identifiable blob, you're sitting too close.

The thing about fringing is that your brain gets used to it, it's almost hard to believe.
When i first got my AW3423DW (1st gen QDOLED) i immediately noticed the fringing on the Aleinware logo when it first turned on. it was TERRIBLE. I could not stop looking for it.

Here's an experiment you should try. Get a monitor that you think has no fringing, then turn it 180 degrees upside down (if you have a monitor arm or if the stand supports it) and change orientation to landscape (flipped). You will notice fringing instantly because now the arangement of the subpixels is different and your brain isn't used to it.

TLDR it's a problem but there is significant brain burn in.
OFC now with the new RGB Stripe QD‑OLED panels should be way better.

comments.text: It's unfortunately not that simple. People talk about how this is an issue with windows and ClearType, and while that's definitely a part of it, the real culprit is actually tyhe subpixel layout of the display. With the current;y available QD-OLED options (not RGB stripe), fringing occurs on high contrast material in general, it's just most noticeable on text because it's static, and of course because of how this is handled by ClearType. But if you use dark mode and look at any high contrast static material for non-text related elements, say even UI elements, you can also see it. It's not typically as noticeable, usually because those static elements are larger. But this is also one of the reasons why greyscale solutions don't actually fix the problem entirely. They minimize the ClearType issues at the cost of blocky and unrefined looking text, but the fringing is still visible and distracting due to the subpixel layout of the display.

I have a 27" monitor with 1,152 zones and zero blooming, so it really does have a black level that’s almost like OLED, but… it also has a huge problem that nobody talks about: you completely kill the highlights when you enable local dimming. (QD-OLED has this problem in some HDR configurations too.) It’s very noticeable, and you lose a ton of detail. I basically never use my monitor with local dimming enabled lol.

In SDR it’s impossible to use, it looks absolutely awful. You have to enable HDR, and even with HDR enabled, watching any SDR content isn’t great because of the loss of highlights. It’s only tolerable with HDR content, but even then you still have that damn loss of highlights. And honestly, between keeping the highlights with higher black levels and losing them in exchange for better contrast, I’ll take the first option.

I can’t wait to get an OLED so I can watch any kind of content in high quality with great contrast and, most importantly, all the highlights preserved. It’ll obviously be a downgrade in terms of HDR since my monitor can reach 1,600 nits, but it’ll be worth it.

I bought an Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDM3 back in May I think, it's a 4k 240hz 32 inch Tandem QD-OLED display. It's fantastic. I live in Australia so I also had trouble deciding on a monitor, for every 10 models the US gets, we get 1 of those, so I'm assuming Tim from Monitors Unboxed just gets sent or imports a lot of monitors that never actually go on sale here.

I've had a tiny bit of VRR flicker in just the loadscreens of some games, but 90% of them don't, and it NEVER happens during gameplay. Also the raised blacks literally never happens under any normal circumstance, you literally have to point a flashlight or have it in direct sunlight at mid day to have an issue, when content is playing you'll rarely notice it.

The problem with OLED, is the only people buying them are the insanely picky high-end users, so that's why we're hearing about so many issues, and seeing to many complaints. If OLEDs were in every household, only like 0.1% of people would ever complain. OLEDs aren't perfect, but compared to LCD displays, they might as well be.

I have a 39" 1440p OLED using an older WOLED panel. I write code 10+ hours a day in dark mode. I do not understand the complaint about text fringing.

VA will have poor color depth. OLED will have some text fringing and some burn in. Screen uniformity lottery across all panel types is a mixed bag. Expectation is the root of heartbreak. If you expect that there is a perfect product, you will be disappointed in the reality that there isn't.

Waiting will almost always be a better option to get a better product down the line. I have a QD-OLED, Asus XG27ACDNG. The only time I notice banding is during some greyish scenes, there will be vertical jailbars on the screen especially if VRR is on. With my monitor and Linux Bazzite setup using VRR made the banding look like it was vibrating the banding back and forth (i think its the classic OLED VRR flicker problem).

Power Cycling the monitor by unplugging the power cables, letting it sit for 10-30 minutes, and powering it back on, then running several pixel cleaning cycles did lessen any banding for me.

For text clarity, I see the issue but only if I put my face close up to the screen. From a normal viewing distance I don't notice the sub pixel issues even with dark mode which I use. But maybe Linux KDE does a better job of matching sub pixel layouts from the OS to the monitor?
